subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: Demand is said to be perfectly inelastic when the PED equals:
options: Minus one
Infinity
One
Zero
questions.explain: Perfectly inelastic demand has a PED of zero, shown by a vertical demand curve where quantity does not respond to price.

questions.q: A necessity good with few substitutes typically has demand that is:
options: Price elastic
Price inelastic
Perfectly elastic
Income inferior
questions.explain: Necessities with few substitutes have inelastic demand because consumers continue buying despite price changes.

questions.q: Demand-pull inflation is best described as inflation caused by:
options: Excess aggregate demand relative to aggregate supply
An increase in the exchange rate
Rising costs of raw materials and wages
A fall in the money supply
questions.explain: Demand-pull inflation occurs when aggregate demand exceeds aggregate supply, pulling the price level up.

questions.q: A good with a PED of -0.4 is described as:
options: Unit elastic
Relatively elastic
Price inelastic
Perfectly elastic
questions.explain: A coefficient between 0 and -1 means demand is price inelastic, so quantity changes proportionately less than price.

questions.q: Which combination represents the components of aggregate demand most likely to fall during a recession driven by low confidence?
options: Imports and saving
Government spending and taxation
Exports and the multiplier
Consumption and investment
questions.explain: Falling confidence reduces consumer spending and firms' investment, the two most cyclically sensitive components of AD.

questions.q: Which policy is an expenditure-reducing measure to correct a current-account deficit?
options: Deflationary fiscal policy that lowers aggregate demand
Depreciation of the currency
Imposing import tariffs
Supply-side reforms to improve competitiveness
questions.explain: Expenditure-reducing policies cut domestic demand (e.g. tighter fiscal/monetary policy) to reduce import spending.

questions.q: Which cost of inflation is described by money losing value so that savers and those on fixed incomes are worse off?
options: Fiscal drag
Shoe-leather costs
Menu costs
A fall in the real value of money and savings
questions.explain: Inflation erodes the real value of money and savings, redistributing income away from savers and people on fixed incomes towards borrowers.

questions.q: Frictional unemployment refers to people who are:
options: Out of work because of the time of year
Unemployed because of a fall in aggregate demand
Unemployed because their skills are obsolete
Temporarily between jobs while searching for new work
questions.explain: Frictional unemployment is short-term unemployment as workers move between jobs and search for suitable vacancies.

questions.q: Real GDP is preferred to nominal GDP as a measure of growth because real GDP:
options: Includes the value of the black economy
Counts only government output
Is always larger than nominal GDP
Is adjusted for inflation/changes in the price level
questions.explain: Real GDP removes the effect of price changes, allowing genuine changes in the volume of output to be measured.

questions.q: The short-run Phillips curve illustrates a trade-off between:
options: Government spending and taxation
Saving and investment
Economic growth and the balance of payments
Inflation and unemployment
questions.explain: The short-run Phillips curve shows an inverse relationship (trade-off) between the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment.

questions.q: The Marshall-Lerner condition states that a currency depreciation will improve the trade balance only if the:
options: exchange rate is fixed by the central bank
income elasticity of imports is less than one
capital account is in surplus
sum of the price elasticities of demand for exports and imports exceeds one
questions.explain: Marshall-Lerner: depreciation improves the current account when the combined (absolute) price elasticities of export and import demand are greater than unity.

questions.q: In the price mechanism, the rationing function refers to:
options: Prices falling to encourage exports
Prices rising to allocate scarce goods to those willing to pay
Prices incentivising producers to supply more
Prices signalling where resources should move
questions.explain: The rationing function uses rising prices to distribute scarce goods to consumers who value them most.

questions.q: Country X can produce both wheat and cloth using fewer resources than Country Y. According to comparative advantage, mutually beneficial trade is still possible provided:
options: both countries fix their exchange rates
Country Y subsidises its exports
Country X has a balance-of-payments surplus
the opportunity-cost ratios of the two goods differ between the countries
questions.explain: Gains from trade arise whenever opportunity-cost (and hence relative-cost) ratios differ, even if one country has absolute advantage in both goods.

questions.q: Export-led growth as a development strategy typically relies on:
options: reducing the savings ratio
fixing prices below market levels
raising import tariffs to protect all home industries
exploiting comparative advantage to expand output sold abroad
questions.explain: Export-led (outward-looking) growth uses trade and comparative advantage to widen markets and raise productivity.

questions.q: The primary remit of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) is to:
options: set tariffs for member states
provide concessional loans only to the poorest countries
finance long-term infrastructure projects
promote global monetary cooperation and provide short-term balance-of-payments support
questions.explain: The IMF oversees the monetary system and lends to members facing balance-of-payments problems, often with conditionality.

questions.q: The expectations-augmented (long-run) Phillips curve suggests that in the long run:
options: The Phillips curve is downward sloping forever
Higher inflation always lowers unemployment permanently
There is a permanent trade-off between inflation and unemployment
Unemployment returns to its natural rate regardless of the inflation rate
questions.explain: In the long run the economy returns to the natural rate of unemployment, so the long-run Phillips curve is vertical with no permanent trade-off.

questions.q: Globalisation has been driven by all of the following EXCEPT:
options: containerisation and improved logistics
rising worldwide tariff barriers
falling transport and communication costs
trade liberalisation and the growth of multinationals
questions.explain: Globalisation has been propelled by falling barriers, cheaper transport/communication and MNCs; rising tariffs work against it.

questions.q: Aggregate demand in an open economy is correctly expressed as:
options: C + I − G + (X − M)
C + I + G + (M − X)
C + S + T + M
C + I + G + (X − M)
questions.explain: AD equals consumption plus investment plus government spending plus net exports, i.e. C + I + G + (X − M).

questions.q: The Claimant Count measure of unemployment counts:
options: People claiming unemployment-related benefits such as Jobseeker's Allowance/Universal Credit
Only those unemployed for over a year
Everyone of working age without a job
Those actively seeking work in a survey of households
questions.explain: The Claimant Count records people claiming unemployment-related benefits, whereas the ILO/Labour Force Survey measure uses a survey-based definition.

questions.q: A subsidy granted to producers will, ceteris paribus:
options: Leave price unchanged
Shift the demand curve to the right
Shift the supply curve to the right and lower equilibrium price
Shift the supply curve to the left and raise price
questions.explain: A subsidy lowers production costs, shifting supply right, increasing quantity and lowering market price.

questions.q: An increase in net migration of skilled workers is most likely to:
options: Shift LRAS to the left
Shift LRAS to the right by increasing the quantity and quality of labour
Reduce the natural rate of growth
Have no effect on productive capacity
questions.explain: A larger, more skilled workforce raises the economy's productive capacity, shifting LRAS (and the PPF) outward.

questions.q: A customs union differs from a free-trade area because members of a customs union also:
options: allow free movement of labour and capital
adopt a single common currency
harmonise all fiscal policy
operate a common external tariff against non-members
questions.explain: A customs union combines internal free trade with a common external tariff, distinguishing it from a simple free-trade area.

questions.q: A normal good that is a luxury has a YED that is:
options: Negative
Greater than one (positive)
Exactly zero
Between zero and one
questions.explain: Luxuries are income elastic with YED greater than one, so demand rises more than proportionately with income.

questions.q: The accelerator theory states that investment depends on:
options: The level of government spending
The rate of interest only
The absolute level of national income
The rate of change of national income/output
questions.explain: The accelerator relates investment to the rate of change of output, so rising demand induces proportionally larger investment.

questions.q: In behavioural economics, 'bounded rationality' refers to the idea that:
options: Consumers always maximise utility perfectly
Firms can never make profit
Markets always clear instantly
Decision-making is limited by information, time and cognitive capacity
questions.explain: Bounded rationality recognises that limited information and mental capacity prevent fully rational optimisation.

questions.q: The terms of trade for a country are best defined as the:
options: index of export prices divided by the index of import prices, times 100
tariff revenue collected on imported goods
value of the current account as a share of GDP
volume of exports divided by the volume of imports
questions.explain: The terms of trade = (index of average export prices / index of average import prices) x 100.

questions.q: Absolute advantage exists when a country can produce a good using:
options: a lower opportunity cost than another country
fewer resources (more output per input) than another country
a higher tariff than another country
a fixed exchange rate
questions.explain: Absolute advantage is about greater productive efficiency (more output per unit of input), distinct from comparative advantage's opportunity-cost basis.

questions.q: Making automatic pension enrolment the default option exploits which behavioural insight?
options: Anchoring
Inertia and default bias
Hyperbolic discounting only
Loss aversion only
questions.explain: Default options exploit inertia, as people tend to stick with the pre-set choice rather than opt out.

questions.q: A positive output gap exists when:
options: Actual output is below the trend rate of potential output
The economy is in a deep recession
Actual output is equal to potential output
Actual output exceeds the productive potential of the economy
questions.explain: A positive output gap occurs when actual real output is above the long-run potential output, typically generating inflationary pressure.

questions.q: In the Keynesian aggregate supply model, the AS curve is horizontal at low levels of output because:
options: The economy is at full employment
Inflation is the binding constraint
Wages are perfectly flexible downwards
There is substantial spare capacity so output can rise without raising prices
questions.explain: With large spare capacity, firms can increase output by employing idle resources without bidding up costs, so the Keynesian AS curve is horizontal.
